video.title: 17 Years, 75 Businesses, 1 Marriage: How We Make It Work

summary: Chris Koerner talks with his wife about the strains and rewards of building businesses as a couple, including a phone repair shop, LCD work, car buying, and a home bakery. They discuss financial uncertainty, trust, backup plans, communication, and making time for family. The conversation also recalls several business concepts and possible future careers, but gives few operating or financial details for most of them. The main practical lessons are to test demand, agree on risks together, and set boundaries around work.

acquisition.how: Agents could manage local pages, content, and paid-ad operations with routine checks. In the UK, software-led outreach must follow PECR; cold email to limited companies is permitted, while individual and sole-trader marketing requires consent.

onboarding.how: A form could collect device and fault details, but a person would need to confirm the diagnosis and repair scope.

delivery.how: Physical device repairs require a person to inspect and handle each phone or tablet.

billing.how: A booking and payment system could automate estimates, invoices, and receipts, with human review of repair-specific charges.

support.how: Agents could answer routine status questions, but repair diagnosis and complaints would need human escalation.

risks: The founders opened a store without testing demand first, and it took months to attract enough business.
A good location did not guarantee walk-in traffic; the shop had to become a destination.

tactics.name: Test demand before committing to a storefront
steps: Start by repairing phones on the side.
Use the small-scale work to prove that local demand exists.
Try paid ads before committing to a full store; the transcript does not specify an ad platform.

quote.text: if it were today, I would have taken my mentor's advice and started fixing phones on the side, proved the demand, tried some paid ads.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Plan for a business downturn
steps: Keep some savings or a job opportunity available as a fallback.
Discuss what the fallback would be before starting, so the risk is shared.

quote.text: I think it's important to have a backup plan, you know, like make sure there's some savings or a job opportunity or or something else that they can fall back on.
quote.speaker: Name not stated

tactics.name: Make business decisions together
steps: Acknowledge when a business decision feels scary to a partner.
Talk through the concern and reconsider the plan together.
Do not start a venture behind a partner's back.

quote.text: I feel like that's something that we have done like I don't you've never done anything behind my back or like started anything that we haven't talked about before which I think is is huge.
quote.speaker: Name not stated

tactics.name: Protect family time from work
steps: Schedule one-on-one time with children and attend important events.
Leave the laptop in the office rather than carrying it around the house.
Set a no-phone rule at dinner.

quote.text: So, if your schedule is so busy that it requires penciling in time to like spend one-on-one time with a kid or make it to an athletic event or whatever, like make sure your family sees that you prioritize that.
